the_unformed_leader.name: The Unformed Leader
the_unformed_leader.description: Your manager means well. That much is clear. But nobody on the team knows what's expected of them, feedback is either absent or arrives as a surprise, and the people who were here before you keep leaving. You've stopped waiting for direction. You've started working around it. The organization is paying to replace people it didn't have to lose, and the ones who stay have quietly lowered what they expect from this place.

the_overloaded_manager.name: The Overloaded Manager
the_overloaded_manager.description: Your manager was good at this job before the team doubled and the scope expanded. Now your one-on-ones are status updates, development conversations don't happen, and when you need a decision you wait. They're not checked out — they're drowning. The organization redesigned the role without redesigning the resources, and the team is absorbing the cost of that mistake.

the_dormant_talent.name: The Dormant Talent
the_dormant_talent.description: Your manager can tell you exactly what you need to grow. They just don't do anything about it. The team's development has stalled while the manager's visibility keeps climbing. People have noticed the pattern. The ones with options are starting to act on it.

built_to_fail.name: Built to Fail
built_to_fail.description: You took this job because it looked like the right next step. Six months in you understand why the last person left. The scope is impossible, the resources aren't there, and when you raise it you're told to figure it out. The person before you was told the same thing. The organization keeps hiring strong people into a broken structure and writing each departure off as a hiring mistake.

the_undefined_role.name: The Undefined Role
the_undefined_role.description: You and your manager don't agree on what your job actually is. Not in a conversation you've had — in the daily reality of what lands on your desk, what gets escalated, what falls through. Work is duplicated in some places and orphaned in others. The organization is paying for a role that isn't doing what anyone thinks it's doing because nobody has said clearly what that is.

the_paper_tiger.name: The Paper Tiger
the_paper_tiger.description: Everyone knows this person shouldn't still be here. The conversations have happened — in one-on-ones, in hallways, in performance reviews that somehow came out fine. The file tells a different story than the one the manager has been telling. When the moment comes to act, the organization discovers it has been managing one employee on paper and a completely different one in practice.

the_founders_grip.name: The Founder's Grip
the_founders_grip.description: Nothing significant moves here without one person's approval. That person is overextended, hard to reach, and making decisions on information that's weeks old by the time it gets to them. You've learned to work around the bottleneck or wait. The senior people who couldn't live with either option have already left.

the_exposed.name: The Exposed
the_exposed.description: There is no functioning HR in this organization. There are employees, obligations, and risk — and nobody whose actual job it is to manage any of it. People with concerns have nowhere to bring them. The organization isn't between HR leaders. It's accumulating liability on a timeline it doesn't know is running.

the_uninitiated.name: The Uninitiated
the_uninitiated.description: Something consequential is coming — a merger, a regulatory event, a restructuring — and the organization has never done this before. The people leading it are capable and underprepared. They don't know what they don't know, and the cost of that gap tends to arrive all at once.

leadership_continuity_risk.name: Leadership Continuity Risk
leadership_continuity_risk.description: Two or three people in this organization carry the relationships, the knowledge, and the institutional memory that keep everything functional. There is no plan for what happens when any of them leave. Everyone knows this is a problem. It hasn't become a priority because those people haven't left yet.

hr_capture.name: HR Capture
hr_capture.description: HR reports to the person it's supposed to provide independent oversight of. If you have a concern about that person, you already know HR isn't where you bring it. The function exists. It cannot do its job from where it sits, and the people who most need it have figured that out.

decision_paralysis.name: Decision Paralysis
decision_paralysis.description: Things get decided in meetings and relitigated in the hallway. You've stopped counting on a decision holding until it actually happens. The cost isn't in any single reversal — it's in everything the organization isn't doing while it cycles through the same conversations without landing.

the_policy_lag.name: The Policy Lag
the_policy_lag.description: The handbook hasn't been touched in years. The law has. People are operating under policies that were compliant when written and aren't anymore. Nobody has noticed because nothing has gone wrong yet. The organization's exposure is real and invisible until it suddenly isn't.

the_unexamined_algorithm.name: The Unexamined Algorithm
the_unexamined_algorithm.description: AI tools are making or influencing employment decisions here — hiring, performance, compensation. Nobody has looked carefully at the criteria they're applying or whether those criteria hold up legally. The efficiency is real. The audit hasn't happened. The two facts are going to meet eventually.

heard_and_ignored.name: Heard & Ignored
heard_and_ignored.description: You reported something. You did it the right way, through the right channel, because you believed it would matter. It didn't. The problem is still present. You're still in the room with it. Everyone who watched what happened to your report has drawn the obvious conclusion about whether the channel is worth using.

the_tolerated_violation.name: The Tolerated Violation
the_tolerated_violation.description: There is a practice in this organization that people know is wrong. It has been known for a while. It continues because the person at the center of it is protected, because addressing it is uncomfortable, or because someone made a quiet calculation that the risk was manageable. Each day it continues that calculation gets harder to defend.

dueling_narratives.name: Dueling Narratives
dueling_narratives.description: Two versions of what happened are circulating and both have organizational authority behind them. People have heard both. They've done the math on which one to believe. The inconsistency is a liability in any proceeding that involves discovery — and a daily tax on the credibility of everyone defending the official version.

the_unsolved_problem.name: The Unsolved Problem
the_unsolved_problem.description: There was a complaint. It was resolved — settled, closed, documented. The behavior that produced it was never addressed. The person affected moved on. The condition didn't. The organization's prior resolution will be exhibit A when the next one surfaces.

transition_paralysis.name: Transition Paralysis
transition_paralysis.description: A leadership change is underway and the organization has stalled around it. People are waiting to see who lands where before they commit to anything. Decisions are being deferred. Initiatives are on hold. The work is accumulating behind the uncertainty while everyone manages the transition instead of doing their job.

paper_shield.name: Paper Shield
paper_shield.description: The policies are current. The training is documented. The acknowledgment forms are signed. None of it reflects what actually happens here. The compliance infrastructure is real on paper and largely decorative in practice. When something goes wrong the paper trail will describe an organization that doesn't exist.

the_lost_map.name: The Lost Map
the_lost_map.description: The information you need to do your job exists somewhere in this organization. It lives in someone's inbox, someone's memory, a system that hasn't been updated, a folder nobody can find. You make decisions without it because finding it takes longer than making the call. The organization is operating on incomplete pictures because nobody has built the architecture to make the right information findable.

invisible_influence_architecture.name: Invisible Influence Architecture
invisible_influence_architecture.description: The org chart shows who has authority. It doesn't show who actually shapes decisions. There are people in this organization whose influence far exceeds their title and others whose title suggests authority they don't have. The real decision-making structure and the official one have separated. Outcomes that nobody can officially explain keep happening anyway.

pay_exposure.name: Pay Exposure
pay_exposure.description: You know you're underpaid. Your manager probably knows too. The organization has looked at the market data and deferred the conversation because fixing it is expensive. The departures it's producing are being explained as career moves, culture fit, better opportunities. The real reason isn't in any exit interview.

the_pay_fog.name: The Pay Fog
the_pay_fog.description: You've compared notes. The numbers don't make sense. Similar roles, different pay, no framework anyone can explain or defend. It wasn't a problem when the numbers were private. Pay transparency requirements are making the incoherence visible in ways the organization isn't prepared for.

the_fracture.name: The Fracture
the_fracture.description: Two leaders at the top of this organization are in open conflict and everyone knows it. You navigate meetings differently depending on who's in the room. Decisions require political calculation rather than judgment. People have chosen sides because the leaders already have. The work that requires both of them to function is the work that isn't getting done.

the_second_close.name: The Second Close
the_second_close.description: The acquisition closed. The integration didn't. You're working inside two organizations that operate under the same name but run on different systems, different assumptions, and different ideas about who's actually in charge. The deal thesis assumed the hard part was the transaction. The people living inside it know otherwise.

silosolation.name: Silosolation
silosolation.description: Your team is hitting its targets. The work that requires another team to hit theirs isn't happening. The problem gets explained as a communication issue, a personality conflict, a specific person who's difficult to work with. It's structural. The same failures keep appearing regardless of who's involved because nobody has addressed what's actually producing them.

the_suppression_filter.name: The Suppression Filter
the_suppression_filter.description: You've stopped telling your manager the full picture. Not because you're hiding anything — because you've watched what happens to bad news in this organization. It gets softened on the way up. By the time it reaches someone who could act on it, it doesn't look like bad news anymore. So you edit. Everyone does. Leadership is making decisions on a version of reality that nobody below them actually recognizes.

the_arbitrary_standard.name: The Arbitrary Standard
the_arbitrary_standard.description: The rules don't apply the same way to everyone and people have noticed. Someone got away with something that someone else was disciplined for. The inconsistency has a pattern. People have decoded it. The organization's ability to hold anyone accountable depends on a fairness that the workforce no longer believes exists.

decision_blindness.name: Decision Blindness
decision_blindness.description: A consequential decision was made without the people who should have been in the room. Legal found out after. HR heard it secondhand. The coordination failure was invisible until something went wrong — and now everyone is looking at who knew what and when, and the answer is uncomfortable.

the_untouchable.name: The Untouchable
the_untouchable.description: There is a specific person in this organization who operates by different rules than everyone else. Complaints have been made. Nothing has changed. The rest of the organization has drawn the obvious conclusion and adjusted accordingly — not just about this person, but about whether the rules mean anything here at all.

what_nobody_says.name: What Nobody Says
what_nobody_says.description: Everyone knows. Nobody says it. The real conversation happens in the parking lot, in the group chat, in the five minutes after the meeting ends. In the meeting everyone says something different. The gap between those two conversations is where this organization actually lives — and where its worst decisions get made, because the people making them don't have the real information.

leadership_deafness.name: Leadership Deafness
leadership_deafness.description: Leadership here genuinely believes they have an accurate picture of what's happening in this organization. They don't. Every layer between them and the work has learned to translate bad news into something easier to deliver. The filtered version is consistent enough that leadership has stopped questioning it. They are managing a picture of the organization, not the organization itself.

the_diversity_ceiling.name: The Diversity Ceiling
the_diversity_ceiling.description: The organization talks about inclusion. The promotion and retention patterns tell a different story. The people who have been passed over know why. The explanations offered don't hold up against the data. The gap between what the organization says it values and what it actually rewards is visible to everyone it affects — and it's shaping decisions about who stays.

culture_drift.name: Culture Drift
culture_drift.description: Something has changed here and nobody made a decision to change it. The organization that exists today isn't the one people joined. The things that made it distinctive — the candor, the pace, the sense that the work meant something — have eroded without anyone being able to point to when it started. People who've been here long enough feel it. They don't always say it.

identity_erosion.name: Identity Erosion
identity_erosion.description: The people who most defined what this organization stood for are leaving. Not all at once — one at a time, with individual explanations that each make sense on their own. The cumulative pattern is something different. The culture isn't drifting. It's being evacuated by the people who carried it, and the organization hasn't named what's happening yet.

the_culture_that_wasnt.name: The Culture That Wasn't
the_culture_that_wasnt.description: The values are on the wall. The culture described in the all-hands is not the culture experienced in the building. New hires figure this out within their first ninety days. Tenured employees stopped expecting alignment a long time ago. Maintaining the official story now requires active effort, and the people being asked to maintain it are running out of reasons to bother.

the_burned_credibility.name: The Burned Credibility
the_burned_credibility.description: Leadership made commitments it didn't keep. The first time it was explained. The second time it was rationalized. By now the workforce has stopped listening to announcements about what's going to be different. The credibility required to lead change has been spent. Initiatives that need people to believe in them are launching into an organization that has already decided not to.

invisible_burnout.name: Invisible Burnout
invisible_burnout.description: The people doing the most critical work are running out of capacity and not saying so. They're not saying so because this organization has taught them that flagging it looks like weakness. They will leave before they complain. The warning signs are there for anyone looking. Most people aren't looking until the resignation letter arrives.

the_basement_standard.name: The Basement Standard
the_basement_standard.description: Underperformance isn't addressed here. Not one person's — the organization's tolerance for it as a pattern. The people who perform know exactly what they could get away with if they stopped. Some of them are starting to do the math. The ones who care most about standards are the ones most likely to leave rather than lower them.

the_inside_track.name: The Inside Track
the_inside_track.description: Performance isn't the primary criterion for advancement here and people know it. The people who get ahead share characteristics that aren't in any job posting. The people who don't have those characteristics have figured out the real criteria and made their own calculations about whether to keep trying or start looking.

narrative_lock.name: Narrative Lock
narrative_lock.description: The organization has an official account of itself and defends it against evidence. People who contradict the official story — even with data — get managed rather than heard. The people holding the narrative have more organizational power than the people who know it's wrong. The cost is in every decision made to protect the story instead of address the reality.

groundhog_day.name: Groundhog Day
groundhog_day.description: This problem has been solved before. The task force ran. The initiative launched. Things improved and then returned to exactly where they were. You've stopped getting excited about the next intervention because you've seen how it ends. The organization keeps treating what's visible and leaving intact what's generating it. Each failed solution makes the next one harder to believe in.

the_wrong_reward.name: The Wrong Reward
the_wrong_reward.description: The behaviors that get rewarded here and the behaviors leadership says it values are not the same. People have run the experiment. They know which set actually matters for advancement, for recognition, for survival. They're optimizing for the real reward system — not the stated one — and the organization is getting exactly the behavior it's paying for.

the_unreported_hazard.name: The Unreported Hazard
the_unreported_hazard.description: There is a safety concern in this organization — physical, psychological, or operational — that hasn't been formally reported. People know about it. The reason it hasn't been reported is itself a finding about what this organization has taught people to expect when they raise concerns.

the_unlocked_door.name: The Unlocked Door
the_unlocked_door.description: A known vulnerability exists and hasn't been closed. Not because nobody has seen it — because the mechanism for addressing it hasn't been used. The organization is aware. It hasn't acted. When something goes wrong, the awareness will matter more than the inaction was ever worth.

the_broken_compass.name: The Broken Compass
the_broken_compass.description: You've been in the meeting where it was diagnosed. You've read the report. You've heard the leadership team agree that something needs to change. That was eighteen months ago. The people with the most options — the ones the organization can least afford to lose — have stopped waiting for the next conversation to be different.

FTA-17.text:
You're reading this and you're not quite sure why.

Nothing is on fire. The team is functioning. Decisions are getting made at reasonable velocity. The people you want to keep are staying. The culture isn't performative — people actually seem to mean it when they say they like working here.

You Googled something anyway. Maybe "signs of organizational health" or "protecting company culture during growth" or something like that. Maybe you took a diagnostic that was designed for organizations in crisis and it told you... you're fine. Which feels right. But also incomplete.

Here's the thing: you're not wrong to be paying attention.

---

## What You've Built

The Anchor is the rarest finding in the diagnostic system. Not because healthy organizations are rare — they're not — but because healthy organizations don't usually go looking for diagnostic tools. They don't need to. Things are working.

You're here anyway. That's interesting.

Most Anchor organizations don't know they're Anchor organizations. They think they're normal. They assume every company has leadership teams that actually align, decision-making processes that actually work, cultures that actually mean something. They don't realize how unusual that is until they talk to someone from outside who tells them "that's not how most places work."

So let's be clear about what you have: coordinated decision-making, low structural friction, engaged leadership, and a culture that produces rather than absorbs. The conditions that break most organizations — the politics, the paralysis, the drift — either aren't present or are being actively managed.

That didn't happen by accident. Someone built it. Someone maintained it. Someone made a hundred small decisions that kept the organization from drifting into the patterns that trap most of its peers.

That someone might be you. Or it might be the leadership team, or the cultural DNA from early hires, or a combination of factors you can't fully separate. Either way: it's real, it's valuable, and it's more fragile than it looks.

---

## The Risk No One Talks About

Healthy organizations fail too. They just fail differently.

The failure mode for an Anchor isn't the dramatic collapse. It's the slow drift. The imperceptible decay. The gradual erosion of the conditions that made the health possible, so slow that nobody notices until the health is gone.

Here's how it usually happens:

**Scale.** The organization grows. New people join. The cultural assumptions that everyone shared when there were forty people don't automatically transmit to the eighty people who weren't there. The decision-making processes that worked at one speed struggle at another. The relationships that made everything function become stretched too thin to carry the same weight.

**Transition.** A founder moves on. A key leader leaves. Someone who was load-bearing in ways nobody fully understood until they were gone is suddenly gone. The organization has to figure out how to do what they did without them — and often discovers that what they did was holding more together than anyone realized.

**Success.** Ironically, this is the most dangerous one. The organization succeeds. The success produces pressure — investor expectations, market expansion, the need to scale faster. The pressure creates urgency. The urgency squeezes out the slack that allowed for the culture maintenance, the relationship building, the things that felt like luxuries but were actually infrastructure.

None of this is inevitable. But it's common. And it's more common in healthy organizations than people admit, because healthy organizations aren't looking for the warning signs. They think they're immune.

---

## What Protection Looks Like

The work for an Anchor organization isn't repair. It's protection. Prevention. The deliberate identification and maintenance of the conditions that made the health possible.

That starts with seeing clearly what you have. Which processes are actually working versus which ones feel like they're working but are held together by specific individuals? What cultural norms are institutionalized versus which ones would disappear if the people who carry them left? Where are the single points of failure — the relationships, the roles, the assumptions — that the organization depends on without realizing it?

Most healthy organizations have never mapped this. They know things are good. They don't know exactly why things are good. That gap is where the vulnerability lives.

The next step is building redundancy. Not bureaucracy — the last thing a healthy organization needs is to process itself into paralysis. But systems that don't depend on any single person's presence to keep working. Documentation that actually captures the way decisions get made. Succession plans that exist before they're needed.

And then there's transmission. How do the cultural norms get to new people? How does the thing that makes this place different survive the dilution of growth? The organizations that stay healthy through scale are the ones that figure out how to make the implicit explicit — how to teach what everyone used to just know because they were in the room.

---

## Why Bother

A reasonable question. Things are working. Why go looking for problems?

Because the cost of losing what you have is much higher than the cost of protecting it.

You've seen what happens to organizations that drift into dysfunction. The decision-making paralysis. The political games. The talent drain. The culture that becomes a punchline on Glassdoor. Getting there is easy. Getting back is hard. Sometimes impossible.

The organizations that stay healthy are the ones that treat health as something that requires maintenance, not something that maintains itself. They do the protection work before it's urgent. They map the conditions before they erode. They invest in the systems before the systems become critical.

That investment feels unnecessary when things are going well. "Why fix what isn't broken?" But things that aren't broken can still be fragile. And fragility, left unaddressed, becomes breakage.

The question isn't whether you can afford to do this work. It's whether you can afford not to.

---

## What's Next

If you're an Anchor organization, you probably don't need an engagement. You need a conversation.

Not about what's wrong — there isn't much. About what you're holding and how you're holding it. About the specific conditions that make this place work and how they'd respond to the pressures you're expecting. About the single points of failure you might not have noticed and the redundancy you might want to build.

It's a different kind of conversation than the one most organizations have with outside advisors. You're not asking for diagnosis. You're asking for protection. For a sharper edge on something that's already working.

That's worth doing. The organizations that treat their health as an asset worth protecting — that stay intentional about the conditions that created it — are the ones that hold it through the transitions that break everyone else.

If that sounds like you — if you're here because you want to protect something rather than fix something — that's a conversation worth having.

Let's talk about what that looks like.

LIB-014.text:
Coordination drag is not a people problem. It is a structural one. When the organization grows past the point where trust and familiarity carry communication, something has to replace them — and that something has a cost.

Anchor is the state that names what happens when a role, a person, or a structure that once worked has not been updated to match what the organization has become. The drag it creates is real — measured in decision velocity, in the initiatives that stall before they start, in the energy spent navigating around something that should not require navigation. What makes Anchor difficult is that the source of the drag is usually not visible as a source. It presents as friction. It gets attributed to process, to communication, to culture. The structure generating it rarely gets named.

This is partly because Anchor states are often occupied by people or roles that were genuinely valuable at an earlier stage. The person who was the right hire at forty employees is not automatically the right person at two hundred. The approval process that made sense when the founding team needed coordination becomes a bottleneck when the organization has built the competency that process was designed to compensate for. The value was real. The fit has changed. The organization has not updated the fit.

The cost of Anchor compounds quietly. Unlike the high-severity states, there is no single dramatic event that forces the question. The organization simply moves more slowly than it should, in ways that are hard to attribute and easy to normalize. High performers learn to route around the drag. The workarounds become standard practice. The standard practice obscures the source. The source continues generating friction while the organization believes it has adapted.

Adaptation is not resolution. An organization that has learned to work around an Anchor has not removed the drag — it has distributed it across every person and process that now incorporates the workaround. The true cost is larger than the friction at the source. It is the accumulated cost of every adaptation, every workaround, every decision routed around the thing nobody has named.

Resolution requires naming it. That is harder than it sounds when the anchor is a person, because naming it requires separating the value the person provided historically from the fit the role requires now. Organizations that cannot hold that distinction — that treat any examination of a long-tenured person's fit as a verdict on their worth — will not resolve an Anchor state. They will manage it indefinitely, at compounding cost, until the drag becomes undeniable or the organization stops growing into the friction.

The diagnostic identifies where the drag is concentrated and what is generating it. Resolution is a structural decision, not a performance management one. The question is not whether someone is doing their job. The question is whether the job, as currently defined, is the right job for where the organization is going.

E7.raw_text: Experiment 7 — Organizational Psychology Literature Review Principal Resolution — PRV3 Research // Experiment 7 of 7 Organizational Psychology Literature Review The final experiment. Five decades of organizational psychology research analyzed for what it establishes about the conditions that produce organizational dysfunction — through what mechanism, and with what measurable effect. The explanatory layer that makes the taxonomy a diagnostic rather than a catalog. This experiment is different in kind from the six that preceded it. The others produced conditions that are recognizable — a leader can read the description and think "that's us." The organizational psychology literature produces conditions that are explanatory — they tell you why the recognizable condition exists and persists. That explanatory layer is what makes the private output more than a diagnosis. It's what makes it a verdict. 10 Research Constructs 10 New Candidates 18 Existing Confirmed 50+ Years of Research Meta Analytic Evidence Why This Experiment Is Different The previous experiments identified what the conditions look like from outside — from employees, from litigants, from practitioners, from actuaries. This experiment establishes what produces the conditions from inside — the causal mechanisms that make organizational dysfunction stable, self-reinforcing, and resistant to the interventions organizations most commonly attempt. 1 Research Construct Role Ambiguity and Role Conflict Foundational Research Kahn et al. (1964) Meta-Analysis Gilboa et al. (2008), n=169 studies Effect Size Among largest in org psych literature What the Research Establishes Role ambiguity — the absence of clear information about what a role requires — and role conflict — incompatible demands within a role — are among the organizational stressors most strongly negatively correlated with job performance. The Gilboa et al. (2008) meta-analysis examined 7 stressors across 169 samples (N=35,265): role ambiguity and situational constraints showed the strongest negative correlations with performance. The meta-analytic evidence confirms this finding across industries, cultures, and organizational types. The Mechanism Role ambiguity is not a personal failing — it is produced by specific structural failures: unclear job descriptions, absent performance criteria, inadequate onboarding, restructuring without role redefinition, and managers who define expectations verbally rather than documenting them. Role conflict is produced by matrix reporting structures, cultures where stated values conflict with operational demands, and performance systems that reward behaviors conflicting with stated priorities. PRV3 Evidence Gilboa et al. (2008) examined 7 organizational stressors across 169 samples (N=35,265): role ambiguity and situational constraints were the two stressors most strongly negatively correlated with job performance. The performance impact is quantifiable before any attrition or claim calculation — a direct input to the Patterned Consequence Logic (the engine framework linking organizational conditions to quantified financial outcomes). Conditions Surfaced New Candidate Role Clarity Deficit Neither the employee nor their manager can specify with precision what the employee is supposed to do, how performance will be evaluated, or what authority they have to act. Systemic condition produced by organizations that restructure without redefining roles, promote into expanded scope without updating expectations, or add responsibilities without removing others. Mechanism for The Unformed Leader — the formation debt produces role ambiguity in the employee below, not just ineffective management above. The cascade is documented in the research literature. Confirms and Explains Decision Paralysis Confirmed. Role conflict from competing decision-making authorities is the mechanism underneath Decision Paralysis — incompatible demands from multiple authority structures produce the paralysis the condition describes. Confirms and Explains Misaligned Incentives Confirmed. Role conflict between stated organizational values and rewarded behaviors is the specific mechanism Misaligned Incentives creates at scale. 2 Research Construct Psychological Safety Foundational Research Edmondson (1999) Major Validation Google Project Aristotle (2016), n=180 teams Finding Strongest predictor of high-performing teams What the Research Establishes Psychological safety — the shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking — is the single strongest predictor of team performance, stronger than team composition, individual talent, or technical expertise. The mechanism is informational, not attitudinal: psychologically unsafe environments suppress information, which degrades decision quality, error detection, and learning speed. The Mechanism Psychological safety is a team-level phenomenon produced almost entirely by leader behavior. One leader who consistently responds to concerns with defensiveness or punishment creates an unsafe environment for their entire team within weeks. The condition spreads through the organization as leaders model the behavior for their reports. The contagion pattern is downward and rapid. Recovery is slow because it requires consistent counter-evidence over extended time. PRV3 Evidence Psychological safety can be measured with Edmondson's validated seven-item instrument. The items are situational rather than self-referential — respondents answer about their team's behavior, not their own feelings. This means the diagnostic can detect psychological safety levels without the user recognizing what is being measured. The P-03 design principle (diagnostic questions observe conditions, users recognize the result, scoring weight invisible to the respondent) is directly satisfied. Conditions Surfaced New Candidate Information Suppression Cascade Low psychological safety has propagated upward through the management hierarchy so that information reaching senior leadership is systematically filtered. Not deliberate deception — each layer has learned not to surface problems. The Executive Reality Gap is the senior leadership experience of this condition. Connects the Executive Reality Gap (conference experiment) to its root mechanism. The research establishes that information suppression cascades are produced by specific leader behaviors — which means the diagnostic question set can identify the cascade from observable signals without requiring the leader to self-report the filtering. Confirms and Explains Psychological Safety Collapse Confirmed across exit interview, Glassdoor, and conference experiments. Now explained: the mechanism is informational, not emotional. The private output should lead with the information quality argument. The organization is making decisions on systematically incomplete data. 3 Research Construct Organizational Justice Foundational Research Greenberg (1987) Meta-Analysis Cohen-Charash & Spector (2001), n=190 studies Key Finding Injustice is a significant upstream driver of turnover intention What the Research Establishes Organizational justice has three components: distributive (are outcomes fairly distributed), procedural (are the processes for making decisions fair), and interactional (are people treated with dignity in those processes). Organizational injustice is a significant direct driver of both turnover intention and job satisfaction — justice perceptions function as upstream inputs that shape satisfaction, which then predicts turnover. The effect is consistent across cultures, industries, and organizational types. The Critical Insight Employees who receive fair outcomes through unfair processes report lower organizational commitment than employees who receive unfavorable outcomes through fair processes. An employee who loses a promotion through a transparent, well-documented process is more committed than an employee who receives a promotion through an opaque, arbitrary one. The process matters more than the outcome — which is the opposite of what most organizations believe. PRV3 Evidence Cohen-Charash and Spector (2001) meta-analysis across 190 studies: organizational injustice is a significant direct driver of both turnover intention and job satisfaction. Job satisfaction remains the primary proximal predictor of turnover, with justice perceptions as an upstream input — not a direct out-prediction of satisfaction. This is the financial consequence mechanism for Process Justice Failure. Conditions Surfaced New Candidate Process Justice Failure Employment decisions made through processes that employees perceive as arbitrary, opaque, or inconsistently applied. Distinct from outcome injustice — the organization may make correct decisions through indefensible processes. The research establishes that process justice failure produces organizational commitment decline and turnover intention independent of whether outcomes are actually fair. This condition is invisible to standard engagement measurement, which asks about satisfaction with outcomes rather than confidence in processes. The PRV3 diagnostic is positioned to detect it specifically because process perception is measurable through situational questions. Confirms and Explains Favoritism Architecture Confirmed. Procedural injustice is the research mechanism underneath Favoritism Architecture — the perception that advancement processes are not transparent or consistently applied is precisely what the organizational justice literature predicts and measures. 4 Research Construct Conservation of Resources Theory Foundational Research Hobfoll (1989) Key Principle Resource loss spirals — loss begets loss One of the most cited frameworks in org stress research What the Research Establishes People strive to obtain, retain, protect, and foster resources — physical, psychological, social, and material. Resource loss is disproportionately stressful relative to equivalent resource gain. When resource loss occurs, people become more vulnerable to future resource loss because the defensive behaviors they adopt consume additional resources. Loss spirals are self-reinforcing: each loss makes the next loss more likely. The Mechanism in Organizations High performers who are losing resources invisibly adopt high-resource-consuming compensation strategies — working longer, covering for others, masking the cost — that accelerate the resource loss while maintaining visible output. The spiral ends in departure or disability. COR theory predicts that high performers leave first during resource depletion: they have the most options when their resources become unrecoverable. PRV3 Evidence COR theory predicts that the organization progressively loses its highest performers first during resource depletion conditions — leaving it progressively dependent on employees with fewer alternatives and lower performance ceilings. This is the financial consequence mechanism for Resource Depletion Architecture: not immediate attrition cost, but systematic degradation of the talent pool. Conditions Surfaced New Candidate Resource Depletion Architecture An organizational design that systematically depletes employee resources faster than the organization replenishes them. Not about individual overload or specific bad managers — a fundamentally extractive organizational structure. Roles expand without narrowing. Expectations increase without resource increases. The organization consumes its human capital faster than it generates it. Explains why The Squeeze (conference experiment) and Invisible Burnout (exit interview experiment) are not random — they are the predictable outcomes of Resource Depletion Architecture. The research gives the diagnostic the causal explanation the practitioner-facing evidence couldn't provide. Confirms and Explains Invisible Burnout Confirmed. COR theory is the mechanism: high performers adopt high-resource-consuming compensation strategies that maintain visible output while accelerating the underlying resource loss. The compensation strategy is what makes the burnout invisible. Confirms and Explains The Squeeze Confirmed. COR theory predicts that simultaneous role expansion without resource addition produces a resource loss spiral by structural design — withdrawal from high-risk activities, defensive compliance, eventual departure. 5 Research Construct Self-Determination Theory Foundational Research Deci & Ryan (1985) Meta-Analysis Van den Broeck et al. (2016), n=99 studies Three Basic Needs Autonomy, Competence, Relatedness What the Research Establishes Human motivation and wellbeing depend on satisfaction of three basic psychological needs: autonomy (volitional control), competence (felt effectiveness), and relatedness (connection). Need frustration — the active blocking of these needs — produces burnout, turnover intention, and counterproductive work behavior beyond the effects of need dissatisfaction alone. The distinction between frustration and dissatisfaction is critical for PRV3. The Mechanism Competence frustration — arbitrary or inconsistent performance feedback — shifts motivation from autonomous (I want to do this) to controlled (I have to do this to avoid punishment) to amotivated (I don't believe my effort matters). The amotivated employee is present, delivering minimum required output, and consuming organizational resources without contributing discretionary effort. This shift is stable and self-reinforcing. PRV3 Evidence SDT research establishes that controlled motivation produces systematically lower performance, creativity, and organizational citizenship behavior than autonomous motivation — even when the controlled and autonomously motivated employees are producing the same observable output. The performance gap is in discretionary effort and innovation, which are unmeasured by most organizational performance systems. Conditions Surfaced New Candidate Motivational Architecture Failure Reward, recognition, and performance management systems have produced a predominantly controlled or amotivated workforce. Not low engagement — a specific psychological condition where the majority of employees either perform to avoid punishment or have stopped believing their effort affects outcomes. Self-reinforcing: organizations with controlled motivation produce more controlling management. Explains why engagement survey scores and productivity metrics can look acceptable while the organization is experiencing significant undisclosed performance degradation. The loss is in discretionary effort and innovation — unmeasured by conventional performance systems and therefore invisible until it produces a crisis. Confirms and Explains The Control Culture Confirmed. SDT establishes that controlling management cultures produce autonomy frustration at scale — the mechanism underneath The Control Culture's organizational outcomes. Confirms and Explains Impossible Standard Confirmed. Competence frustration through inconsistent or arbitrary performance standards is the SDT mechanism that produces amotivation — the endpoint of the Impossible Standard condition. 6 Research Construct Social Identity Theory and Organizational Identification Foundational Research Tajfel & Turner (1979) Key Insight Organizational identity is a source of self-concept Implication Culture change is identity threat What the Research Establishes People derive part of their identity from group memberships and act to maintain positive distinctiveness of those groups. Organizational identification — the degree to which employees define themselves through their organizational membership — predicts organizational citizenship behavior, commitment, and resistance to organizational change. Organizational identification is produced and destroyed by organizational conditions — it is not a stable individual trait. The Mechanism Organizational changes that appear to threaten the organizational identity reduce identification and produce resistance that is rational from the employee's perspective — they are protecting a source of their self-concept. Culture Drift is not just a behavioral change — it is an identity threat. Post-acquisition resistance is not irrational — it is identity-protective behavior. The resistance to change that organizations label as irrational is often a predictable identity-protection response. Conditions Surfaced New Candidate Identity Erosion The organizational identity that employees joined and identified with has changed substantially enough that current employees no longer recognize themselves in the organization's stated identity. Not Culture Drift (behavioral norms) — specifically the core organizational identity: what the organization is for, what it stands for, who it serves. The employees who leave are not just disengaged — they are deidentified. Explains the specific mechanism of post-pivot attrition: employees who joined a mission-driven organization that has become commercially-driven are not leaving because of dissatisfaction — they are leaving because the organization no longer provides the identity resource they joined it for. The private output for this condition should name this mechanism directly. Confirms and Explains The Second Close Confirmed. Social identity research explains why integration efforts that acknowledge and honor the acquired organization's identity succeed more often than those that don't — reducing the identity threat reduces the resistance that produces integration failure. Confirms and Explains Change Absorption Failure Confirmed. The resistance to organizational change that organizations label as irrational is often identity-protective behavior — which means change management that acknowledges identity threat will be more successful than change management that treats resistance as ignorance. 7 Research Construct Moral Disengagement Foundational Research Bandura (1999) Eight Mechanisms Including euphemistic labeling, diffusion of responsibility, dehumanization Key Insight Produced by organizational conditions, not individual pathology What the Research Establishes Moral disengagement comprises eight mechanisms through which individuals disable the self-regulatory processes that normally keep behavior aligned with moral standards. These mechanisms are not individual pathologies — they are produced by organizational conditions. Organizations that structure accountability diffusely, use euphemistic language for harmful practices, and create competitive pressure that makes harmful behavior seem necessary systematically produce moral disengagement across their workforce. The Mechanism in Organizations Sequential Decision Blindness (from the litigation experiment) is explained by the diffusion and displacement of responsibility mechanisms — each decision-maker believes someone else holds the accountability. Normalization Creep is explained by euphemistic labeling and advantageous comparison — harmful behavior is relabeled and compared favorably to worse behavior until it becomes morally invisible. The organizational conditions produce the mechanism; the mechanism produces the behavior. Conditions Surfaced New Candidate Organizational Moral Drift Moral disengagement mechanisms embedded in the organizational culture. The language of the organization has shifted to euphemistically label harmful practices. Responsibility for consequences has been diffused across enough decision-makers that no individual feels accountable. Competitive comparison justifies practices that would otherwise be recognized as harmful. Distinct from Normalization Creep — this is systemic, not behavior-specific. The most severe presentation of this condition produces the organizational environment in which whistleblower events, regulatory investigations, and public scandals become inevitable — because the internal moral regulation mechanism has been disabled at the organizational level. Internal Reporting Failure (litigation experiment) is the specific consequence of Organizational Moral Drift at the governance layer. Confirms and Explains Sequential Decision Blindness Confirmed. The diffusion and displacement of responsibility mechanisms explain why no individual in the organization acts with retaliatory intent while the sequence constitutes retaliation. The mechanism is structural, not individual. Confirms and Explains Normalization Creep Confirmed. Euphemistic labeling and advantageous comparison are the Bandura mechanisms that make harmful behavior morally invisible over time — the gradual process the Normalization Creep condition describes. 8 Research Construct Psychological Contract Theory Foundational Research Rousseau (1989) Meta-Analysis Zhao et al. (2007), n=51 studies Critical Distinction Breach (cognitive) vs. violation (emotional) What the Research Establishes The psychological contract — the individual employee's beliefs about the terms of the reciprocal exchange with their employer — produces more severe responses when violated than formal contract violations, because the violation involves perceived betrayal rather than legal dispute. Psychological contract breach predicts organizational citizenship behavior decline, job satisfaction decline, and organizational commitment decline. The Critical Distinction for PRV3 The research distinguishes breach (cognitive recognition that a promise hasn't been kept) from violation (emotional experience of betrayal). Organizations that acknowledge breach produce breach without violation. Organizations that are silent about unmet commitments produce violation.
